say.text: Time to build your one-pager. You choose what goes on it; I only check it.
Five quick picks, then your review cards.
Pick the best 'basics' line for the top of your TOF page.

choices.label: Most common cyanotic CHD; four parts: VSD, overriding aorta, RVOT obstruction, RVH
Most common cyanotic CHD; four parts: VSD, ASD, overriding aorta, RVOT obstruction
Most common cyanotic CHD; four parts: VSD, overriding aorta, RVOT obstruction, LVH

say.text: The right-sided ventricle has to push against the obstructed outflow. Which ventricle thickens, and is a second septal defect part of the four?
Yes. TOF is the **most common cyanotic congenital heart disease**, and classic TOF has a large VSD, an overriding aorta, infundibular RVOT obstruction and **right ventricular hypertrophy**.
**Pentalogy of Fallot** is TOF plus an **atrial septal defect**, so the ASD sits outside the four.
Tempting: ASD is a septal defect, and an ASD does get attached to TOF in the pentalogy.
But the four are a large VSD, an overriding aorta, infundibular RVOT obstruction and RVH. ASD makes it **pentalogy**.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so lock this in: TOF plus ASD is pentalogy of Fallot, never the classic four.

say.text: Tempting: hypertrophy is in the name of the finding, so the wrong ventricle slips in.
The component is **right ventricular hypertrophy**, as the RV pushes against the RVOT obstruction. LVH is not one of the four.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so pause on this: the fourth component is right, not left, ventricular hypertrophy.

say.text: Now the one line that explains the colour. Which goes on your page?

choices.label: Tighter RVOT obstruction means more blood bypasses the lungs, so bluer
The bigger the VSD, the bluer the child
If RVOT resistance is below systemic resistance, the child is deeply blue

say.text: Ask which structure sets how much blood reaches the lungs: the hole or the outflow?
Yes. With significant RVOT obstruction, most blood shunts toward the aorta, bypassing the pulmonary bed.
Presentation varies with the severity of RVOT obstruction. Resistance across the RVOT below systemic resistance means minimally cyanotic or acyanotic: the pink Tet.
Tempting: the VSD is the visible hole, so it seems to set the shunt.
But the clinical presentation varies with the severity of **RVOT obstruction**. Significant obstruction sends most blood to the aorta, away from the lungs.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so remember: it is the outflow obstruction, not the VSD size, that sets the blueness.

say.text: Tempting: the numbers are the right ones, but the direction is flipped.
If resistance across the RVOT is **less** than systemic resistance, the patient is minimally cyanotic or acyanotic.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so flip it back: low RVOT resistance means pink, not blue.

say.text: Next, the imaging line. Which is correct for your page?

choices.label: Boot-shaped heart is a classic X-ray sign; echo is the gold standard
Boot-shaped X-ray confirms TOF; echo is only a backup

say.text: A sign you can see on film and the test that is the gold standard are not always the same test.
Yes. Chest films may classically show a **boot-shaped** heart with an upturned apex from RVH.
But the **echocardiogram** is the gold standard and the primary diagnostic modality.
Tempting: 'classic sign' sounds like 'confirmatory test'.
The boot is only a classic X-ray possibility. The **echocardiogram** is the gold standard.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so note the split: boot = classic sign, echo = gold standard.

say.text: The tet spell card. Which step goes with the reason 'increase systemic vascular resistance'?
A spell pushes blood away from the lungs; the fix raises resistance in the systemic circuit. Which option does that, with no drug?
Yes. **Knee-chest positioning**, to increase systemic vascular resistance.
Tempting: vasodilating sounds like easing the strain on the heart.
The listed spell steps do the opposite: knee-chest to increase SVR, and **IV phenylephrine** to increase systemic afterload.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so remember: the logic is to raise systemic resistance, never lower it.

say.text: Tempting: a blue, struggling child looks like failure that needs a diuretic.
But the listed steps are knee-chest, oxygen, **IV fluid boluses** to improve RV filling, IV beta-blockers, IV phenylephrine and morphine.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so note this: spell management adds fluid to fill the RV, it does not remove it.

say.text: Pair another. Which step goes with 'pulmonary vasodilation'?
Yes. **Oxygen**, to cause pulmonary vasodilation.
Close, it is on the spell card, but its job is different: **phenylephrine** increases systemic afterload.
Oxygen is the one for pulmonary vasodilation.
Close, it is on the card too, but fluid boluses improve RV filling.
Oxygen is the one for pulmonary vasodilation.
Last pair. Which reason goes with IV beta-blockers?

choices.label: Decrease heart rate and aid RV filling further

say.text: Yes. **IV beta-blockers**, to decrease heart rate and aid RV filling further.
That reason belongs to phenylephrine.
Beta-blockers slow the heart rate and aid RV filling further.
That is morphine, given as a sedative in a spell.
Beta-blockers slow the heart rate and aid RV filling further.
A repaired TOF child returns years later. Write the line: commonest reason to reoperate?
Think of what the repair leaves behind at the pulmonary valve, not the lesions it closed.
Yes. **Pulmonary insufficiency** is the most common indication for reoperation after repair.
Tempting: the VSD was the original hole, so a leftover feels likely.
The answer is **pulmonary insufficiency**, the most common indication for reoperation.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so recall: after repair, the valve leaks, not the VSD patch.

say.text: Tempting: the obstruction was the original problem, so it might return.
But the most common indication for reoperation is **pulmonary insufficiency**.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so remember: pulmonary insufficiency tops the list.

say.text: Without surgery, what is the most frequent cause of death? Add it to the page.
You just built the spell card. The commonest killer is the event it treats.
Yes. Without surgery: **hypoxic spells (68%)**, cerebrovascular accidents (17%), brain abscesses (13%).
It is a real cause, but second: 17%.
Hypoxic spells lead at 68%.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so fix the order: spells 68%, strokes 17%, abscesses 13%.

say.text: It is a real cause, but the smallest of the three: 13%.
Hypoxic spells lead at 68%.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so fix the order: spells 68%, strokes 17%, abscesses 13%.

say.text: That is your one-pager: the four parts, the outflow idea, echo as gold standard, the spell card, pulmonary insufficiency and hypoxic spells.
Your review cards follow.

cards.q: Most common cyanotic congenital heart disease?

cards.a: Large anteriorly malaligned VSD, overriding aorta, infundibular RVOT obstruction, RVH.
TOF plus an atrial septal defect.

cards.q: What decides how blue a TOF child is?
cards.a: Severity of RVOT obstruction: significant obstruction shunts most blood to the aorta; resistance below systemic means minimally cyanotic.
Echocardiogram; the boot-shaped heart is only a classic X-ray possibility.
Knee-chest (raise SVR), oxygen (pulmonary vasodilation), IV fluids (RV filling), IV beta-blockers (lower heart rate), IV phenylephrine (raise afterload), morphine (sedation).

cards.q: Commonest indication for reoperation after repair?
Commonest cause of death without surgery?
cards.a: Hypoxic spells (68%), then cerebrovascular accidents (17%), brain abscesses (13%).
